rows.wylie: gzhan yang , dpal chos kyi grags pa'i lung dang khyod 'gal ba yin te, khyod kyi nad lnga dang , 'byung ba lnga dang , gdon lnga dang bcas pa rnams, nyon mongs pa dug lnga'i dngos 'bras su khas blangs, mu stegs byed kyi bad kan dang 'dod chags rgyu 'bras, mkhris pa dang zhe sdang rgyu 'bras sogs su khas blangs pa la, bad kan dang 'dod chags rjes su 'gro ldog 'khrul, mkhris pa dang zhe sdang rjes su 'gro ldog 'khrul pas de 'gog byed kyi, 'khrul phyir rlung sogs chos ma yin, , zhes pa'i gzhung 'don pa sgyur ba'i sgo nas khyod la gnod pa'i phyir dang , 'dus ma byas kyi nam mkha' phrag dog gi dngos 'bras su 'dod pa mi rigs pa'i phyir
rows.english: And anyway, maybe it's you who have contradicted a statement of the glorious Dharmakirti. You have taken the position that the five sicknesses, and the five elements, and the five demons are all the direct result of the five poisons--the five bad thoughts. But when the non-Buddhists take the position that phlegm and desire have a cause-and-effect relationship, and that bile and anger have the same kind of relationship, and so on, then Master Dharmakirti refutes them by showing that desire doesn't always come and go according to the phlegm, and anger doesn't always come and go according to the bile. To do so he makes the statement that says, "It's not a fact that wind and the rest are such, for the relationship doesn't always hold." We could twist around this statement too and say that it disproved your position; and add as well how wrong it is to assert that uncreated space could ever be the direct result of jealousy. [The point seems to be that, although your position about the bad thoughts, and our original position on the nature of the three beings' perceptions, are both correct, you could always twist around some quotation by a master, take it out of context or misinterpret it, and try to show they were wrong.]

rows.english: And anyway, maybe it's you who have contradicted a statement of the glorious Dharmakirti. You have taken the position that the five sicknesses, and the five elements, and the five demons are all the direct result of the five poisons--the five bad thoughts. But when the non-Buddhists take the position that phlegm and desire have a cause-and-effect relationship, and that bile and anger have the same kind of relationship, and so on, then Master Dharmakirti refutes them by showing that desire doesn't always come and go according to the phlegm, and anger doesn't always come and go according to the bile. To do so he makes the statement that says, "It's not a fact that wind and the rest are such, for the relationship doesn't always hold." We could twist around this statement too and say that it disproved your position; and add as well how wrong it is to assert that uncreated space could ever be the direct result of jealousy. [Translator's note: The point seems to be that, although your position about the bad thoughts, and our original position on the nature of the three beings' perceptions, are both correct, you could always twist around some quotation by a master, take it out of context or misinterpret it, and try to show they were wrong.]

rows.acip: KHA CIG NA RE, KHYOD DNGOS PO'I DNGOS 'BRAS YIN NA, KHYOD YIN NA DNGOS PO'I DNGOS 'BRAS YIN PAS KHYAB ZER NA,

rows.english: Suppose someone else comes and says: If something is the direct result of a working thing, then if something is it, then that something must be the direct result of the working thing.

rows.acip: DNGOS PO'I PHYI LOGS SU BYUNG BA CHOS CAN, KHYOD YIN NA DNGOS PO'I DNGOS 'BRAS YIN PAS KHYAB PAR THAL, KHYOD DNGOS PO'I DNGOS 'BRAS YIN PA'I PHYIR,

rows.english: Let's consider the working thing that comes in the next moment after a working thing. Are you saying that—if something is this working thing of the next moment—then it has to be the direct result of the working thing? Why do you say that? Because, after all, that something is the direct result of the working thing.
